entry.title: fix(serve): /health says what is waiting, not how many jobs it has ev…
entry.content:
fix(serve): /health says what is waiting, not how many jobs it has ever seen

`queue` reported `len(self.library.jobs)`, which is every job the process has created
since it started and is never pruned. So a healthy box that had served a hundred builds
said `queue: 100`, and a box with a hundred waiting said the same, and an operator had
no way to tell them apart.

It is the number that would have shown targum-internal#228 — every chat turn hanging
until four dead workers left the queue growing with nobody on it — and it could not.
Live tonight it reads 172, which means nothing under either reading.

Two numbers now: `queue` is `queue.qsize()`, what is actually waiting, and `jobs` is
what it has seen. `deploy.sh` greps for `"ok": true` and is unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(sefaria): Rashi on the Chumash is refused for what is missing, no…
entry.content:
fix(sefaria): Rashi on the Chumash is refused for what is missing, not for an edition

`<Who> on <Name>` claimed everything with a name, so `sefaria:Rashi on Genesis` went to
the daf reader, asked Sefaria for the Vilna edition — which exists for tractates and not
for the Chumash — and came back "Sefaria has no 'Vilna Edition' of Rashi on Genesis".
True, and about the wrong thing. Sefaria holds several editions of it, one of them
public domain; what targum lacks is a reader for a commentary numbered by chapter and
verse, where a verse carries a comment or several (targum-internal#200).

So the daf module declines a subject that is a book of the Tanakh, and `sefaria.py` says
the true thing in its own words, naming what it does read. Nothing is asked of Sefaria
on the way, which the test pins: the old path spent a request to be told the wrong
answer.

entry.title: fix(mail): a sign-in link in a language that is not English arrives w…
entry.content:
fix(mail): a sign-in link in a language that is not English arrives whole

The body falls back off 7-bit whenever it is not ASCII, which is every word of a
Russian or Hebrew email (targum-internal#186). What it fell back to was unnamed, so the
encoder picked 8bit: raw UTF-8 on the wire, safe only where the whole SMTP path
advertises 8BITMIME, and mangled or refused where it does not — in the one email that
is the entire product working or not.

Base64 instead, named. Quoted-printable is the other 7-bit-safe candidate and it puts
the soft break back inside the sign-in token, which is exactly what `cte="7bit"` on the
line above exists to avoid; base64 wraps too, but a client decodes it whole before it
looks for a link, so the token arrives in one piece.

Tested through the mailer's own `_deliver` rather than a copy of it: `compose` in the
test file rebuilds the message the way the mailer does, which tests the intention, and
the two new tests hold the mailer to it. The subject was already right — `EmailMessage`
does RFC 2047 on its own — and is pinned, because the day that stops being true is the
day a Russian reader gets a subject line of mojibake.

entry.title: test: the private half is checked wherever it exists
entry.content:
test: the private half is checked wherever it exists

Eight modules are gitignored and ship in the wheel. CI has a public checkout and never
sees them; a worktree of a tracked branch does not carry ignored files either, and
worktrees are where most work here happens. So nothing checks them, and they depend on
the public half: a rename in `recording/`, `weekly/index.py` or `models.py` breaks one
while every check stays green, and it surfaces at the next weekly build, by hand
(targum-internal#230).

`tests/test_private_half.py` imports each of the eight where it is present and skips
where it is not, which is the bargain `needs_dicta_model` already makes about a model on
disk. It also refuses a half-copied checkout: some of them present and some missing is
somebody's interrupted copy, and the weekly would fail on whichever is absent rather
than say so here. Nine pass in the main checkout; eight skip everywhere else.

The names are written down rather than discovered, so a private module quietly
disappearing fails a test instead of being one less thing checked. `CLAUDE.md` gains the
command, beside the worktree note that explains why it is needed.

Found by running ruff in the main checkout for the first time: three import-order errors
had been sitting in the private half unseen. Fixed there, where a gitignored fix travels
in the wheel rather than in a commit.

entry.title: test: the suite is offline because it is stopped, not because it is a…
entry.content:
test: the suite is offline because it is stopped, not because it is asked nicely

`conftest.offline` said the suite stayed offline and only skipped the two tests carrying
the `network` marker. Everything else was trusted, and on 2026-09-08 the trust turned
out to have lapsed: when the fetch door stopped being httpx's, three tests in
`test_ssrf.py` went on patching `httpx.Client.stream`, intercepted nothing, and made
real requests to example.com. The checks between a reader's pasted link and a hosted
box's metadata endpoint had stopped running and the suite was green
(targum-internal#229).

So the promise is enforced. An outbound connection to anything but loopback fails with
a sentence saying what the test did, and so does a knock on the real fetch door, which
connects inside libcurl where a socket patch cannot see it. The door may still be
*built*, because `_open` makes its client before it checks the address and refusing the
build would fail every test of an address that is turned away before anything leaves.

Measured before the rule went in: of ~2,900 tests, five reached out, and all five were
one thing — `needs_dicta_model` checks the weights are on disk and skips otherwise, but
the loader still asked Hugging Face whether its cache was current. `HF_HUB_OFFLINE` is
set at conftest import, beside the catalogue line and for the same reason a fixture is
too late. `test_weekly_verify` runs in 7 seconds rather than 78; the round trip was most
of it.

The guard is tested, since a guard nobody tests is the shape of the thing it replaced:
a refused connection, a refused knock, a door that may still be built, loopback left
alone, and the marker still skipping.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Merge branch 'egress' — the fetch door is a browser's, and the proxy …
entry.content:
Merge branch 'egress' — the fetch door is a browser's, and the proxy is the exception

targum#128 and the `egress` branch answered targum-internal#226 independently and
arrived at nearly the same design: the same knob with YouTube's as its fallback, the
same retry-only-on-a-refusal rule, the same `via` on what came back, the same schema 15
column recording which way out a knock went. #128 landed first and is the weaker half.

The branch probed from the box, which #226 said had never been done, and the probe
changes the premise: six of the seven Hebrew hosts are not refusing our address. They
serve Cloudflare's bot check to any client whose TLS handshake is not a browser's, and
the laptop and the box get the identical answer. A proxy does not open those. A
browser's handshake does, so the door is `curl_cffi` impersonating Chrome, it knocks
politely, a challenge is named as one to the model rather than reported as silence, and
the proxy is retried only over https, where TLS is end-to-end through CONNECT.

Taken from the branch: the door, the challenge, the politeness, the https rule, and the
corrected record of what those seven hosts actually do. Taken from master: everything
merged since the branch point, which `--theirs` on a whole file would have dropped —
the shelf's read times, the build's words option, the whole-web search, and the parasha
and daily preflight lines. Dropped from #128: its `check_fetch_egress`, whose hosted
message promised a proxy would open hosts a handshake opens; `Store.egress_of`, which
nothing calls; and its tests, which the branch's own cover.

Three things the branch had not finished, fixed here rather than left: `curl_cffi`
ships no stubs so the session wanted an annotation, two test lines ran long, and — the
one that matters — `tests/test_ssrf.py` and two download tests still patched
`httpx.Client.stream`. After the swap those stubs intercepted nothing, so the redirect,
size-cap and redirect-limit tests were making real requests to example.com and passing
on its 404. They patch the door's own seam now.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(fetch): a host that refuses this address is tried once more thro…
entry.content:
feat(fetch): a host that refuses this address is tried once more through the egress

Seven of the 42 Hebrew hosts probed on 2026-09-07 refuse the caller rather than the
client — a browser User-Agent gets the same 403 — and one of them is the Ministry of
Education's news in easy Hebrew, which is the best learner text found anywhere.
Nothing installed here answers that: the request has to leave from somewhere else
(targum-internal#226).

`TARGUM_FETCH_PROXY` is that somewhere, read per call so unsetting it is the whole
rollback, with YouTube's knob as the fallback — one account, two knobs, because an
article is half a megabyte where a video is hundreds. The direct attempt always
happens first and only a refusal is retried, so a 404 stays a 404 and is not paid for
twice. `download()` never goes through it: a gigabyte-scale proxied fetch is the one
thing here that could make a bill surprising.

What came back says which door it came through. `Fetched.via` and `Unreachable.via`
carry it, the chat records it on the host, and `reached.egress` keeps it — because
"the site is reachable" and "the site is reachable from the egress we pay for" are two
different facts, and so are "refuses us" and "refuses us even from there". Schema 15,
additive, and a row written before it reads `direct`, which is what it was.

The client is handed the proxy explicitly and trusts no other: httpx honours
`HTTP_PROXY` by default, which would route every fetch through a variable nobody meant
as a targum setting while `via` still said direct — a bill and a lie at once.

`targum preflight` gains a `fetch egress` line beside YouTube's, redacting the
credentials a residential proxy carries in its URL.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(annotate): a lemmatizer that answered no words has still read the…
entry.content:
fix(annotate): a lemmatizer that answered no words has still read the text

Two scripture tests build an annotation with a stub that answers a key per segment
and nothing in it, and the check refused them. It was asking the wrong question: a
lemmatizer that answers is one that read the text and found nothing in it, which can
be true of a real text. A lemmatizer that answers nothing at all was never in a
position to read it, and that — every segment skipped before it, or by it — is the
blank book this refuses.

entry.title: fix(annotate): a text no word of which could be read is refused, not …
entry.content:
fix(annotate): a text no word of which could be read is refused, not written blank

Two rules leave a block without tokens rather than let a model at a language it does
not know: `unread`, and `ScriptureLemmatizer`, which skips Aramaic the tagging cannot
place instead of handing it to the Hebrew fallback. Each is right about its own block.

Neither is right about a document where every block goes that way. What gets written
then is a reader in which not one word can be tapped, by a build that reported
success — and Targum Onkelos is exactly that shape, which is why it is still not on
the shelf (targum-internal#65). Measured today rather than read: the Onkelos path
returns an empty annotation for every verse, with no error anywhere.

`ScriptureLemmatizer.reads` predicted it in as many words — a whole book "would come
out blank with nothing saying why". This says why, where the Stanza path already
refuses a language it has no models for, and in that path's own words: build it
without --words and read it with the translation only.

A document with nothing to read in it — numerals, punctuation — is not refused, and a
single unreadable block among readable ones is still only a gap.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
